paragraphs: Active learning tries to reduce the number of labels a learner must request. This paper addresses the agnostic setting, where the available hypothesis class need not contain a perfectly accurate predictor. Its algorithm applies to any hypothesis class with bounded VC dimension and permits arbitrary data distributions, giving it a broad theoretical scope.

The method extends an earlier active learning scheme through reductions to supervised learning. These reductions let it use supervised learning procedures as components, while generalization bounds guide the active learning process. The contribution is a way to organize label selection around existing learning machinery without imposing the strong distributional assumptions that restricted much previous work.

The guarantees distinguish dependable behavior from potential savings. A fallback bound controls label complexity by the agnostic PAC sample complexity. Stronger asymptotic improvements hold for certain hypothesis classes and distributions, rather than universally. Experiments also demonstrate improvements. Together, these results support a broadly applicable framework whose label savings depend on the learning problem.
neurips-2007-a-general-agnostic-active-l.tldr: An agnostic active learning algorithm offers a general fallback label bound and achieves label savings for certain hypothesis classes and distributions.

paragraphs: Boosting builds a predictor through successive improvements, but complex training objectives can make those improvements difficult to compute. This paper extends functional gradient boosting to handle such loss functions within a general optimization framework. Its purpose is to connect complicated learning objectives with standard regression learners that are already practical to use.

The central device is a quadratic upper bound on the loss. Instead of working directly with the full complexity of the objective at each stage, the method optimizes these bounds. This construction supports a rigorous convergence analysis and allows a regression base learner, such as a decision tree, to fit the updates required by different loss functions.

The authors apply the framework to ranking search results, combining preference information with labeled examples during training. These provide two forms of supervision within the ranking problem. Experiments using data from a commercial search engine report significant improvements over some existing methods. The evidence supports the framework's usefulness for this application, alongside its broader methodological contribution.
neurips-2007-a-general-boosting-method-a.tldr: Quadratic upper bounds extend boosting to complex losses and yield improved web search ranking in the reported experiments.

paragraphs: Automatic relevance determination, or ARD, removes irrelevant features to produce sparse models. Although effective, popular optimization rules can be slow or lack convergence guarantees. This paper develops an alternative way to optimize a general ARD objective, addressing both the practical computation and the mathematical understanding of feature selection.

The method introduces an auxiliary function that leads to a sequence of reweighted L1 optimization problems. These problems can be handled with standard convex programming tools. The resulting algorithm is efficient and guaranteed to reach a stationary point; this guarantee does not imply that it finds a global optimum. The analysis also interprets earlier fixed-point updates as solving a particular min-max problem iteratively.

A second contribution recasts ARD as MAP estimation with a prior whose weights are coupled and whose form depends on features and noise. This interpretation gives a tighter approximation to the L0 sparsity measure than the L1 norm. The results explain aspects of existing ARD behavior and suggest alternative objectives and update procedures for sparse feature selection.
neurips-2007-a-new-view-of-automatic-rel.tldr: ARD can be optimized through reweighted L1 problems with stationary-point convergence and interpreted through a coupled, feature-dependent sparsity prior.

paragraphs: Related supervised learning tasks may share structure that helps them generalize and may make new tasks easier to learn. This paper proposes a framework for discovering that shared structure. It uses regularization based on spectral functions of matrices, making the mathematical properties of a matrix central to how relationships among tasks are encouraged.

The framework has computational as well as theoretical components. The authors develop an efficient alternating minimization algorithm, which optimizes different parts of the problem in turn. They also establish a necessary and sufficient condition for the regularizer to be convex. Concrete instances connect the general construction to regularization using Lp matrix norms.

Experiments on two real datasets indicate that the algorithm handles increasing numbers of tasks well and improves on the statistical performance of the compared state of the art. These findings support learning task structure through spectral regularization. The potential to help with new tasks motivates the framework, while the stated empirical findings concern scaling and predictive performance on the evaluated datasets.
neurips-2007-a-spectral-regularization-f.tldr: Spectral matrix regularization provides an efficient framework for learning shared task structure, with convexity theory and encouraging results on two datasets.

paragraphs: Dynamic routing concerns how a neural system changes which inputs communicate with which outputs. This paper proposes a neurobiologically plausible model in which that routing depends on neuronal coherence. The key idea is to control the timing relationship between background oscillations so that the appropriate input and output units communicate.

The architecture separates three roles: receiving raw input, controlling routing, and producing an invariant output. Units in the middle tier align the oscillation phases of the input and output tiers to establish the desired mapping. This makes phase coordination an explicit mechanism for selecting communication paths within the model.

An example implemented on a neuromorphic chip achieves circular-shift invariance, meaning that circularly shifting the input can preserve its output representation. The authors also describe a simple extension that can perform circular-shift dynamic routing with O(N) connections, compared with O(N²) for traditional models. The demonstrated invariance and proposed connection savings concern this specific routing setting, supporting a concrete computational role for neuronal coherence.
neurips-2007-an-in-silico-neural-model-o.tldr: A neural routing model uses oscillation-phase alignment to achieve circular-shift invariance, with an extension requiring only linearly many connections.

paragraphs: Recovering a person's three-dimensional pose and body shape from images requires both a useful body representation and a way to fit it automatically. Earlier approaches often used simple articulated parts, struggled with initialization, and assumed known body dimensions. This paper combines direct image-based prediction with subsequent generative refinement to address those difficulties.

The body is represented by a parameterized triangular mesh learned from human range scans. A discriminative model, specifically a conditional mixture of kernel regressors, predicts the mesh's pose and shape parameters from a single image. These predictions then initialize a generative model that performs more detailed estimation. The first stage supplies a starting configuration for the second.

The resulting system supports fully automatic recovery from monocular and multiple-camera imagery. Reported experiments show robust estimation of articulated pose, body shape, and biometric measurements such as height and weight in calibrated and uncalibrated camera environments. The contribution is an integrated route from an image to a detailed body model, with automatic initialization built into the estimation process.
neurips-2007-combined-discriminative-and.tldr: Direct image-based prediction initializes a detailed generative body model for automatic recovery of human pose, shape, and biometric measurements.

paragraphs: Pedestrian detectors can struggle when a person's configuration is uncommon in their training data, such as when someone is mounting a bicycle. This paper investigates whether explicitly estimating body configuration can improve detection. The approach makes pose estimation part of the detector rather than relying only on the appearance of an image window.

For each window, a discriminative procedure first estimates the most likely human pose. This procedure is trained through structure learning on a small dataset. The estimated configuration then determines features passed to an SVM classifier, including local histograms of oriented gradients and local principal components of gradients. Pose therefore influences how the classifier receives evidence about the candidate person.

Experiments on the INRIA Person dataset show that configuration estimates significantly improve detection accuracy. This finding supports using estimated body arrangement to inform a discriminative pedestrian classifier. The demonstrated result is improved overall accuracy on that dataset; the motivation is the difficulty posed by configurations that appear infrequently in training.
neurips-2007-configuration-estimates-imp.tldr: Estimating human pose before extracting classification features significantly improves pedestrian detection accuracy on the INRIA Person dataset.

paragraphs: This paper introduces Relaxed Survey Propagation, or RSP, for finding MAP configurations in Markov random fields. A MAP configuration is a joint assignment of variables with the highest probability under the model. The task requires choosing variables together, because relationships among them affect which complete assignment is most plausible.

The authors assess RSP against several established inference methods: max-product belief propagation, sequential tree-reweighted max-product, residual sum-product belief propagation, and tree-structured expectation propagation. This comparison places the proposed algorithm alongside different approaches to inference in related graphical models. The central evidence is comparative performance on the problems studied.

RSP outperforms all of these compared approaches on Ising models with mixed couplings and on a web person disambiguation task. The latter is formulated as supervised clustering, connecting the inference method to a problem of separating references to people on the web. These results establish favorable empirical performance in both the stated model setting and an applied clustering task, rather than a universal guarantee across Markov random fields.
neurips-2007-cooled-and-relaxed-survey-p.tldr: Relaxed Survey Propagation outperforms the compared inference methods on mixed-coupling Ising models and a web person disambiguation task.

paragraphs: Constraint satisfaction problems ask for assignments that obey a collection of constraints. Constraint propagation uses those constraints to restrict possible assignments. This paper proposes constraint propagation relaxation, or CPR, which gives a probabilistic treatment of that process and uses it to reinterpret a family of survey propagation algorithms.

The family is indexed by a parameter, rho. At rho equal to zero, it corresponds to belief propagation; at rho equal to one, it corresponds to pure survey propagation. CPR supplies another way to understand the entire family between these endpoints. Its contribution is therefore a common conceptual account of algorithms connected by this parameter.

The authors emphasize that the interpretation makes fundamental, previously implicit assumptions behind the family more explicit. Clarifying those assumptions helps explain its effectiveness and leads to applications beyond k-SAT. The stated significance is explanatory and methodological: understanding the basis of survey propagation can guide its use in a wider range of constraint problems, rather than treating it only as a procedure associated with one problem class.
neurips-2007-cpr-for-csps-a-probabilisti.tldr: A probabilistic view of constraint propagation clarifies the assumptions behind the survey propagation family and enables applications beyond k-SAT.

paragraphs: This paper shows that log-linear grammars containing latent variables can be trained practically with discriminative methods. Latent variables provide hidden distinctions within the grammar, while discriminative training focuses on choosing the desired analysis of an observed sentence. Combining them creates a computational challenge because training must account for those hidden alternatives.

The key technique is hierarchical pruning. It makes the feature expectations needed by gradient-based training efficient to approximate, allowing the training procedure to handle the latent grammar. The authors also compare L1 and L2 regularization. In their comparison, L1 needs fewer iterations to converge and produces sparser solutions, with fewer retained nonzero parameters.

On full-scale treebank parsing experiments, the discriminatively trained latent models outperform comparable generative latent models and discriminative models without latent variables. These comparisons support the value of combining hidden grammatical structure with discriminative learning. The practical contribution is the pruning procedure that makes this combination trainable, alongside evidence favoring L1 regularization in the studied setting.
neurips-2007-discriminative-log-linear-g.tldr: Hierarchical pruning makes discriminative latent-variable grammar training practical and improves parsing over the reported generative and non-latent comparisons.

paragraphs: The two eyes see slightly different images, and their displacement provides information about depth. Yet natural scenes contain a much wider range of binocular disparities than the preferred disparities of a population of cortical neurons. This paper addresses the resulting need to recognize when a stimulus falls within the population's useful disparity range.

The authors derive a statistical feature from the responses of V1 disparity neurons to help determine whether the disparity lies within that range. When optimized using natural images, the feature has an interpretation in terms of normalization, a common model of V1 processing. The same feature is then used to support disparity estimation in natural images.

The proposed model produces more correct estimates than the compared coarse-to-fine, multiple-scale approaches and can identify occluded regions. These findings connect confidence about the neural population's operating range with more robust estimation. They also suggest an additional role for normalization: helping a disparity system judge which image regions support a reliable estimate.
neurips-2007-estimating-disparity-with-c.tldr: A statistically derived feature interpretable as neural normalization helps assess disparity range, improve disparity estimates, and identify occlusions.

paragraphs: Finding a graphical model's most probable joint assignment is the MAP inference problem. This paper introduces an approximation algorithm with a message-passing structure similar to max-product. Its distinguishing property is that it always converges, addressing a central difficulty with using max-product as a dependable inference procedure.

The algorithm comes from block coordinate descent applied to a dual formulation of a linear programming relaxation of MAP. In practical terms, its message updates follow an optimization construction rather than requiring a manually chosen step size or tree weights. The paper also extends the approach to cluster-based potentials, broadening the kinds of interactions that the method can represent.

Convergence and exactness are separate claims here. The method always converges, while recovery of the exact MAP solution is proved for various settings. Tests on synthetic and real-world problems compare favorably with previous approaches. The contribution combines an explicit optimization foundation, freedom from the listed tuning parameters, and empirical evidence of useful inference performance.
neurips-2007-fixing-max-product-converge.tldr: An optimization-derived message-passing algorithm always converges and provably recovers exact MAP solutions in various settings without step-size or tree-weight tuning.

paragraphs: GRIFT studies visual classification by asking which image features can explain human performance. Its goal is to recover those features from human data across different classification tasks. This makes the model a tool for investigating the information people use when making visual judgments, as reflected in their observed task performance.

The central modeling choice is to combine multiple feature detectors. Earlier methods represented performance through a single linear classifier acting directly on image pixels. Allowing several detectors gives the model a way to describe classification as the combined contribution of distinct features, rather than compressing the explanation into one linear pixel-based decision.

The authors report that this approach extracts more information about human visual classification than previous methods. The significance lies in the richer explanation it can recover from behavioral data: multiple detected features can contribute to the account of performance. The paper presents this model as a foundation for further exploration of visual classification, with feature recovery as its central contribution.
neurips-2007-grift-a-graphical-model-for.tldr: GRIFT models human visual decisions through multiple feature detectors to recover richer explanations of classification performance from behavioral data.

paragraphs: When classifying objects in a relational database, relationships can help share information between their labels. A common representation places an undirected edge between related objects in a Markov network. This representation makes a particular assumption: given input features and neighboring labels, an object's label is independent of the remaining labels.

This paper examines another explanation for symmetric relationships: objects may be connected because of an unobserved common cause. The authors discuss how the resulting graphical model differs from a Markov network and how it represents different kinds of relational processes. The choice of representation therefore expresses an assumption about why related objects exhibit dependence.

The authors build a Bayesian nonparametric classification model around this common-cause representation and evaluate it through several empirical studies. The contribution is both a modeling perspective and an implemented classifier. It expands the set of assumptions available for relational learning, showing how hidden shared causes can serve as the basis for using relationships in prediction.
neurips-2007-hidden-common-cause-relatio.tldr: A hidden-common-cause representation offers an alternative to Markov networks and supports a Bayesian nonparametric classifier for relational data.

paragraphs: HM-BiTAM jointly models word alignment and the topics underlying paired documents in two languages. Word alignment identifies which words correspond across languages. The paper's central idea is that these correspondences should reflect the topical context of the documents, rather than being learned without the semantic connections between their sentence pairs.

The model couples parallel sentence pairs through a semantic flow that maintains topical coherence. Likelihood-based training learns both topic-dependent translation lexicons and topic representations for each language. The construction combines HMM-based IBM translation models with the bilingual topic admixture approach, connecting a conventional alignment component with explicit bilingual topic modeling.

The trained model can display topic patterns in bilingual collections and provides a principled approach to context-dependent translation inference. The authors report an extensive empirical analysis covering word alignment, bilingual topic representation, and translation. The contribution is a unified account of these three tasks, in which document context helps organize the relationship between words and their translations.
neurips-2007-hm-bitam-bilingual-topic-ex.tldr: HM-BiTAM jointly learns bilingual topics and word alignments so that translation can account for coherent document-level topical context.

paragraphs: Monotonic transformations change the scale of data while preserving order. They can be useful before classification, but choosing them often involves manual experimentation or domain knowledge. This paper learns such transformations automatically together with a large-margin classifier, making the preprocessing choice part of the supervised learning problem.

The learned transformation is a monotonic piecewise linear function, followed by a linear hyperplane classifier. The authors develop two implementations. The first alternates between quadratic and linear programs and converges to a locally optimal solution. The second uses a convex semidefinite relaxation to overcome initialization difficulties in the greedy optimization procedure.

Experiments demonstrate the usefulness of learned transformations on synthetic problems, text data, and image data. The approach matters because the representation and classifier are fitted together, so the transformation can be chosen for the classification objective. Its optimization claims remain specific: the alternating procedure reaches a local optimum, while the improved formulation addresses initialization through a relaxation.
neurips-2007-learning-monotonic-transfor.tldr: Jointly learning monotonic data transformations and a large-margin classifier automates useful preprocessing, with two optimization formulations and empirical demonstrations.

paragraphs: An fMRI recording contains activity measurements from thousands of voxels across time, making prediction and interpretation difficult. This paper compares global and local prediction methods using linear and nonlinear dimensionality reduction. It uses data from the Experience Based Cognition competition to study how compact representations can support prediction of natural experience.

The authors build low-dimensional representations and learn time series whose future values are predicted from fMRI data alone. They find effective models using principal components within anatomically defined Brodmann Areas. This connects dimensionality reduction with recognizable brain regions, making the predictive representation easier to interpret than a description based only on a large collection of individual voxels.

For some stimuli, the strongest predictive regions remain stable across subjects and episodes. Reported examples include Wernicke's area for verbal instructions, visual cortex for face and body features, and Brodmann Area 7 for velocity. These qualified findings support anatomically organized, low-dimensional decoding as a transparent foundation for more sophisticated methods.
neurips-2007-locality-and-low-dimensions.tldr: Low-dimensional models within anatomical brain regions effectively predict aspects of natural experience, with stable predictive regions for some stimuli.

paragraphs: This paper develops multilayer generative models that combine Markov random fields with deep directed belief networks. The aim is to capture natural image patch statistics while retaining efficient learning and inference. The architecture combines interactions within hidden layers with directed influence from higher layers, bringing both forms of structure into one model.

Each hidden layer has its own Markov random field. Connections from the layer above modulate that field's energy function, so the higher layer changes the distribution governing the layer below. Training proceeds one layer at a time. After learning, a very fast inference procedure computes a good approximation to posterior distributions across all hidden layers.

Generating data follows a different procedure: each layer must settle to equilibrium under its top-down input before generation proceeds through the hierarchy. The authors show that these models capture the statistics of natural image patches well. Their contribution is a hierarchical construction that pairs expressive within-layer dependencies with efficient layerwise learning and fast approximate posterior inference.
neurips-2007-modeling-image-patches-with.tldr: A directed hierarchy of Markov random fields captures natural image patch statistics with layerwise training and fast approximate inference.

paragraphs: Optimistic Linear Programming, or OLP, learns to maximize average reward in an unknown Markov decision process. The analysis assumes that the process is irreducible. The algorithm estimates the environment from accumulated experience, then chooses actions by considering favorable transition probabilities that remain close to those estimates.

This optimistic choice is computed through linear programs. It gives the learner a way to act on both its current estimates and the possibility that nearby alternatives offer better rewards. The authors prove that its expected total reward by time T falls short of the optimal policy's reward by at most C(P) log T, with an explicit constant depending on the environment.

The paper also clarifies tradeoffs with related algorithms. Compared with the Burnetas–Katehakis approach, OLP is simpler, avoids needing transition-support knowledge, and has a simpler proof, but its regret bound has a larger constant factor. Compared with the Auer–Ortner approach, it is simpler and has a better dependence on the size of the decision process.
neurips-2007-optimistic-linear-programmi.tldr: OLP uses optimistic linear programs to achieve logarithmic expected regret in unknown irreducible Markov decision processes.

paragraphs: Many models of decision-making assume that evidence can be gathered without a finite deadline. Under that assumption, an optimal policy can wait until evidence reaches a fixed threshold. This paper studies decisions that must instead finish before a deadline, whose timing may be uncertain because of external constraints or imperfect internal timing.

The authors formulate the problem as sequential hypothesis testing with a stochastic horizon and analyze it using dynamic programming. For a large class of deadline distributions, the Bayes-optimal policy uses an evidence threshold that decreases monotonically over time. In these settings, the amount of evidence required to commit becomes smaller as time passes.

Numerical simulations illustrate the policy for a fixed deadline and for a deadline drawn from a gamma distribution. The result gives a decision-theoretic explanation for changing evidence requirements under time pressure. Its scope is conditional on the analyzed deadline distributions: the paper establishes declining thresholds for a broad class, rather than asserting that every uncertain deadline produces the same policy.
neurips-2007-sequential-hypothesis-testi.tldr: For a broad class of uncertain deadlines, optimal sequential decisions use evidence thresholds that decline over time.

paragraphs: This paper derives a simpler online learning rule for information bottleneck optimization with spiking neurons. The derivation relies on suitable assumptions, especially linearization. Under that construction, the new rule performs as well on common benchmark tasks as a previously proposed, more complicated rule, while being easier to interpret mathematically.

The simpler form makes theoretical analysis of convergence feasible. Changing signs in the rule produces a theoretically grounded method for principal component analysis with spiking neurons. Applied to an ensemble, this version can extract different principal components of the input, connecting the learning rule to a familiar way of identifying major patterns of variation.

The framework can also favor components that are related, or unrelated, to an additional target signal. This adds a way to select patterns according to their connection with another source of information. Possible biological interpretations of the target include proprioceptive feedback, other sensory inputs, or top-down signals. These are proposed interpretations, while the learning-rule derivation remains tied to its stated assumptions.
neurips-2007-simplified-rules-and-theore.tldr: Under suitable assumptions, a simple spiking-neuron learning rule supports information bottleneck optimization and a PCA variant guided by target relevance.

paragraphs: This paper extends the sparse pseudo-input Gaussian process model to binary classification. Sparse pseudo-input methods use a compact representation to reduce computation. The authors exploit the model's prior covariance structure to derive a numerically stable training algorithm while aiming to preserve a faithful approximation to the posterior distribution.

Training has O(NM²) complexity, the same asymptotic order as related sparse approaches such as the informative vector machine. Within that computational order, the proposed method represents the posterior more faithfully. The contribution therefore concerns the quality of the approximation as well as efficiency, rather than claiming a better asymptotic training cost than those methods.

Across several benchmark problems, the reported results show that very sparse representations can retain accuracy in many cases. Pseudo-input locations are learned by gradient ascent on marginal likelihood. The authors also identify situations where that optimization is likely to fail and suggest alternatives. The practical message combines substantial possible sparsity with a specific caution about how pseudo-inputs are selected.
neurips-2007-the-generalized-fitc-approx.tldr: A sparse Gaussian process classification method improves posterior representation and often preserves accuracy with high sparsity, while identifying pseudo-input optimization failures.

paragraphs: Reward-modulated spike-timing-dependent plasticity combines a local synaptic learning rule with a reward signal. It is a candidate mechanism for explaining how changes at individual synapses can produce behaviorally useful adaptation in networks of spiking neurons. This paper addresses the need to understand when such learning will produce an intended effect.

Earlier investigations of the rule's potential and limits relied on computer simulations. The authors provide tools for an analytic treatment, allowing conditions for a desired learning effect to be predicted theoretically. This changes the kind of question that can be answered: the analysis can identify when learning should work, rather than only observing outcomes in simulated cases.

As a concrete application, the framework yields a theoretical explanation and a computer model of an experimental finding involving biofeedback in monkeys. The contribution links a candidate synaptic mechanism to a behavioral learning result through mathematical analysis and modeling. Its claim is conditional: the tools characterize circumstances supporting a desired effect, rather than guaranteeing successful adaptation in every spiking network.
neurips-2007-theoretical-analysis-of-lea.tldr: Analytic tools identify conditions for successful reward-modulated STDP and support a theoretical model of a monkey biofeedback finding.

paragraphs: This paper studies optimization directions with generalization in mind. It asks which direction maximizes a reduction in generalization error, or maximizes the probability of avoiding an increase in that error. From both Bayesian and frequentist perspectives, this analysis can lead to the natural gradient direction.

Computing that direction can be expensive, so the authors develop TONGA, an efficient online approximation to natural gradient descent. The aim is to make the approach suitable for large-scale learning. The method connects a theoretical motivation based on performance beyond the training data with an approximation intended to make the resulting optimization procedure practical.

Reported experiments show much faster convergence than stochastic gradient descent in both computation time and iteration count, including on very large datasets. These are empirical optimization results. The generalization-based derivation explains why the authors investigate the direction, while the experiments establish the reported speed advantage. Together, the contributions provide a motivation for natural gradient updates and an efficient way to approximate them online.
neurips-2007-topmoumoute-online-natural-.tldr: TONGA efficiently approximates natural gradient descent online and converges much faster than stochastic gradient descent in the reported experiments.

paragraphs: TrueSkill Through Time extends Bayesian skill ratings from sequential updates to estimates of entire skill histories. Each player's skill at a given time is linked to relevant game outcomes and to skill variables at neighboring times. Smoothing allows later observations to inform earlier skill estimates, producing a connected account of development over time.

The model uses approximate message passing in a factor graph and retains uncertainty estimates, explicit treatment of draws, support for multiple competitors, and inference of individual skills from team outcomes. It also introduces player-specific draw margins, allowing the model to represent differences between players in their tendency or ability to produce draws.

Applied to 150 years of chess history, the approach produces lifetime skill curves and comparisons between players across time. The results indicate an increase in overall playing strength over that period. They also show significantly better predictive power when the model accounts for a player's ability to force a draw, supporting that addition to the skill representation.
neurips-2007-trueskill-through-time-revi.tldr: Temporal smoothing reconstructs chess players' skill histories, while player-specific draw modeling significantly improves predictive power.
